transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2027-06-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Tom Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Halcyon VP Platform), Liam O'Connor (Halcyon Head of ML), Dana Brooks (Halcyon Infra)

Summary: Quick discovery on dedicated/reserved GPU needs, isolation and burst patterns. Customer is evaluating tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted and Dedicated, leaning towards Dedicated for data isolation and latency guarantees, wants a short benchmark + pilot.

Topics: dedicated sizing, warm pools, prewarm latency, KMS/encryption and VPC requirements, fallback to hosted, SLA expectations, benchmark plan, timeline for pilot.

--- Transcript (automated, medium quality) ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, I run this account. With me is Tom, our SE.
[00:07] Priya: Hi, Priya here. Thanks, Maya. We've got Liam and Dana on the line too.
[00:10] Tom: Hey all. Quick check, are there any slides we should reference? Maya: I shared the capacity matrix link in the calendar but we'll keep this free form.
[00:18] Liam: Sounds good. High level — we're building real-time clinical summarization and some ingestion pipelines, so latency matters. We're evaluating dedicated nodes because of PHI and residency.
[00:28] Priya: Yeah, compliance is a hard requirement. We're SOC2 in progress and need KMS integration, and also VPC peering for our pilot.
[00:36] Dana: From infra side, we need to restrict egress and ensure tenant fencing; we don't want noisy neighbor effects.
[00:41] Maya: Totally. Can you give us a sense of expected QPS, avg tokens, and the burst profile? That'll drive dedicated sizing.
[00:48] Liam: Right now tests are small but production could be up to 120 qps sustained during day with spikes to 600 qps for a few minutes. Average request is about 600 tokens in, 150 tokens out, but some flows hit 2k tokens occasionally.
[01:05] Tom: OK so there's a heavy tail on sequence length; KV cache reuse should help if requests are conversational. Are you doing stateless single calls or multi-turn chat with context?
[01:14] Priya: Mostly single-turn summarization from document blobs, so KV cache reuse is minimal. That's why we worry about throughput and prewarm.
[01:21] Maya: Understood. So two axes: isolation (dedicated pools) and burst handling (prewarm/hot pools or burst to hosted). What's your tolerance for increased p95 latency during big bursts?
[01:31] Dana: We need p95 under 400ms for the majority of calls; p99 can be higher but we want to avoid minutes-long queuing — acceptable fallback is to route to a cheaper hosted path with redaction, but only if privacy checks are satisfied.
[01:44] Liam: Important note: any fallback flow must not send raw PHI to 3rd-party hosted models unless encrypted/filtered.
[01:50] Tom: We can configure fallback policies — canary to hosted with a redaction step, or use reserved extra capacity for critical tenants. On Dedicated we can reserve warm nodes and allow burst capacity via dedicated burst pool or our Hosted overflow with customer-approved path.
[02:04] Priya: How quick does a warm node respond? If we have a cold start, that's a big latency hit.
[02:09] Tom: Cold starts are a function of model size and whether KV cache is prepopulated; for a 13B style model on RTX A40 equivalent, a prewarmed worker will return first token latency around 60–120ms depending on sequence length. Cold worker that needs to load weights can take up to 30–90 seconds unless we've preloaded.
[02:25] Priya: 30–90s is unacceptable for user-facing flows. What's the prewarm strategy?
[02:29] Maya: We recommend a warm-pool with stickiness: keep a baseline count of workers running during peak hours and autoscale in small increments, plus a burst reserve we commit to for your contract. We can also do scheduled prewarm before expected surge windows.
[02:41] Liam: If we commit to reserved GPUs, can we guarantee they're isolated to our tenancy?
[02:45] Tom: Yes — Dedicated provides tenancy isolation; your reserved GPUs are on isolated nodes and we offer tenant fencing options. Network-wise we can colocate in your VPC for Private deployment options as well.
[02:55] Dana: What's the difference between Dedicated and Private here? We want the management plane separate but not fully on-prem.
[03:00] Maya: Dedicated is reserved capacity in our cloud with dedicated pools; Private is a deployment option where the control plane and/or nodes can run in your VPC or on-prem. For SOC2 and data residency, customers often pick Private, but Dedicated plus VPC peering is enough for many.
[03:12] Priya: We need KMS/HSM integration for key wrapping, audit logs for model inputs, and SSO with SCIM for user management.
[03:19] Tom: We support KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) and can route customer-managed keys for stored artifacts. Audit logs can be shipped to your log collection. SCIM/SSO is supported.
[03:28] Liam: Good. Back to sizing — what's the unit economics for reserved vs ondemand nodes? We need to model cost per 1M tokens.
[03:36] Maya: I'll share the detailed pricing worksheet, but high-level reserved reduces the per-token compute charge by ~35–50% depending on commit term and model family. There are also quantization profiles that reduce memory and increase packing efficiency.
[03:47] Dana: Can we pin to a quantized variant for cost predictability? Some of our evals showed small quality delta.
[03:52] Tom: Yes you can pin model variants; Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization / batch sizes per workload. We also run quality monitors to flag regressions by prompt set.
[04:01] Priya: For benchmarking — what does a Redwood benchmark look like? We want reproducible results and the ability to run our own harness.
[04:07] Tom: We'll provide a bench harness: runs can simulate token mix, sequence length distro, concurrency, and return latency percentiles. We usually run 1) capacity-scaling test 2) burst simulation 3) KV cache warmup tests. We can share the harness repo and you can run it in your environment against a trial.
[04:24] Liam: For burst sim, can you do realistic spikes (600 qps for 3–5 min) while also running background traffic?
[04:29] Tom: Yep, that's the typical test. We recommend a dry-run on a small model first, then full-size. We'll instrument traces and token-level cost.
[04:36] Priya: About failover: if Reserved pool is saturated, how quickly can we fall back to hosted? And how is data handled in that path?
[04:44] Maya: Failover is near real-time — routing happens within seconds via policy. Data handling depends on config: we can redact or hash inputs before sending to hosted, or you can approve a routed path that uses customer-managed endpoints. We'll include the options in the proposal.
[04:56] Dana: Any preemption risk for our reserved nodes? Eg. are they evicted for higher tiers?
[05:01] Tom: Reserved nodes are non-preemptible. We have ephemeral pools for spot-like capacity but reserved committed nodes are guaranteed.
[05:06] Liam: Good. Next steps?
[05:08] Maya: I'll put together: 1) pricing + reserved SKU mapping, 2) benchmark plan and proposed dates, 3) security and compliance packet (SOC2 scope, KMS config, audit export). Tom will prepare the benchmark harness.
[05:20] Priya: We will produce traffic histograms and confirm the primary tenant list for pilot.
[05:25] Dana: Also include network diagram requirements for VPC peering.
[05:28] Tom: Noted. Any blockers on timeline to run a pilot in two weeks?
[05:32] Liam: If we can get pricing and bench plan quick, likely yes. We aim to start pilot week of 2027-06-28.
[05:38] Maya: Great — I'll send the proposal by Wednesday 2027-06-16.
[05:42] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[05:44] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up with notes and the next meeting invite.

--- End transcript ---
